1.support: Purpose: To assess whether partitioning the elastance of the respiratory system (ERS) between lung (EL) and chest wall (ECW) elastance in order to target values of end-inspiratory transpulmonary pressure (PPLATL) close to its upper physiological limit (25 cmH2O) may optimize oxygenation

2.support: We report patients with influenza A (H1N1)-associated ARDS referred to the Molinette Hospital (University of Turin) for ECMO in the period from September 2009 to January 2010

3.support: In the period October 2009-January 2010, 36 patients with novel A (H1N1) infection were admitted to the ICUs of the Piedmont region. Among them, 20 patients had ARDS and 14 were transferred to the regional coordinating center

4.support: 14 were transferred to the regional coordinating center with ECMO facilities as a result of developing the pre-established criteria. Values of oxygenation index and of PaO2/FiO2 ratio indicated immediate use of ECMO in all patients

5.support: No sample size calculation, power estimate, or discussion of statistical power is reported anywhere in the article; the series comprises 14 patients (7 per group).

6.support: If values of PPLATL during conventional ventilation were less than 25 cmH2O, PEEP was further increased until PPLATL was equal to 25 cmH2O. ECMO criteria were hence evaluated 20-30 min after the initiation of ventilation with the new PEEP setting

7.support: The pressure required to distend the chest wall was estimated using the measurement of esophageal pressure (PES) [20]. ERS, ECW, and EL were calculated as previously described

8.support: No blinding of outcome assessors is described; the physiological outcomes (PEEP, PPLATL, oxygenation index) were assessed by the treating team applying the esophageal-pressure-guided protocol.

9.support: All 14 enrolled patients have data at both time points (Tables 1-3); this is a short-term physiological pre-post study with no patients lost between baseline and post-PEEP-change assessment.

10.support: Comparisons were performed using paired and unpaired T test, as appropriate. Differences were considered significant if P < 0.05. Raising PEEP ... P = 0.0001) to approach the upper physiological limit ... improved oxygenation index (from 37.4 ± 3.7 to 16.5 ± 1.4

11.support: Outcome measures were recorded once during conventional ventilation and once (20-30 min later) after the PEEP change; a repeated-measures interrupted time-series design was not used.

12.support: The intervention (esophageal-pressure-guided PEEP setting) was applied and assessed at the individual patient level, not at a group level.

nih.rationale: The study is a prospective physiological pre-post series with a clearly stated question, prespecified eligibility criteria, a consistently delivered and clearly described esophageal-pressure-guided PEEP titration, objective and validated outcome measures (PPLATL, oxygenation index), complete short-term follow-up, and appropriate paired statistical tests with p values (items 1,2,3,4,6,7,9,10 = Yes). It is rated no higher than Fair because of the very small sample with no power consideration (item 5 = No), lack of blinding of outcome assessors (item 8 = No), and a single before-after measurement per patient rather than a time-series design (item 11 = No), all of which limit confidence that the observed oxygenation improvement is attributable solely to the intervention.
